title: When the sword is right
hookLine: the Zafarnama says that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword (Zafarnama 22)

cards: Winter. A city has been under siege for months. The men outside swore solemn oaths, on what they held holiest, that the people inside could leave in safety.
The oaths broke the moment they stepped outside. In the weeks that followed, the man who led them lost all four of his sons. Almost everything, gone in a single winter.
Then he sat down and wrote a letter to the emperor behind it all. Today: when the sword is right.

teach.b: The man is Guru Gobind Singh. The winter is 1704 into 1705. After the siege of Anandpur and the broken oaths, his two elder sons died fighting at Chamkaur.

His two youngest, still small boys, were executed at Sirhind. Tradition says the Guru wrote the letter soon after, in Persian verse, the language of the Mughal court, and sent it to the emperor Aurangzeb.
It's called the Zafarnama, the letter of victory. A strange title after so much loss.

teach.h: THE VICTORY IS MORAL, NOT MILITARY.
teach.b: But the victory it claims isn't on a battlefield. It's moral. The letter doesn't beg, and it doesn't rage.

It calmly reminds the emperor of the oaths his men swore, and says a ruler who breaks his word has lost something no army can win back. And one couplet, number twenty-two in the usual numbering, sets out a principle.

teach.h: ONLY WHEN EVERY OTHER MEANS HAS FAILED.
teach.b: In plain words: when every other means has been tried and has failed, it is right to take hold of the sword. Notice where the weight falls. Not on the sword.
On everything before it: talking, petition, patience, agreements.
Every other means. The sword is not the first answer. It's the last one, and only when the others are truly used up.

That's the line Sikhs point to when people ask how a tradition of prayer can carry a blade. Force isn't forbidden, but it has to earn its place by coming last. Most days, of course, the question never reaches the sword.
It stops at the next conversation, the next try.

how: Sikhs cite the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh's Persian letter to Aurangzeb, for the principle that force is justified only as a last resort, after every other means has failed.

games.q: you've lost your city and your sons to broken oaths. you write to the emperor. what do you say?
o: calmly name the broken oaths, and set out when force is right.
games.why: the Zafarnama neither begs nor rages. it names the broken oaths and says force is right only when every other means has failed.

practice: Think of a conflict in your life that's stuck, one you may have already decided to fight out, go cold on, or give up.

Before you do, run through the other means: have you asked plainly, listened fully, put it in writing, asked someone to help, waited a day? Find one peaceful way you haven't really tried yet, and picture yourself trying it.

wordCard.voice: Zafarnama, the letter of victory. Its principle: the sword is right only when every other means has been tried and has failed.

orig.note: Gurmukhi spelling of a Persian title: zafar, victory; nama, a letter or book.

carryVoice: Your line: every other means first. The sword, if ever, comes last. That's day two hundred seventy-seven.
